Issue of passports without police verification 
*483 MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that passports have got to be issued within 
35 days even without police verification; 
(b) whether this gives a chance for hardened criminals to get passports 
without police verification; 
(c) the steps Government propose to take to eliminate issue of passports 
to anti-social, anti-national and criminals; and 
(d) the number of cases detected involving Indian Nationals in possession 
of double passports during past three years? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH) 
(a) and (b) Passports are normally issued  within five weeks, provided a clear 
police verification report has been recei ved and the application is complete 
in all other respects. Short validity passports, of an urgent nature, can be 
issued on the basis of a verification certificate issued by an officer not below 
the rank of Deputy Secret ary to the Government of India. Some of the 
Passport Offices have been authorized to issue passports on police report 
overdue basis if the police report is not received within 4 weeks. Whenever a 
negative police report is received, subsequent to issue of the passport, the 
applicants are contacted for clarification and where necessary their passports 
are revoked-impounded. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2001] 
(c) The police verification is designed to ensure that passports are not 
issued to undesirable elements. Government have strengthened scrutiny of 
documents submitted in support of passport applications, as well as the 
police verification process. 
(d) The information is being collected and will be laid on the Table of the 
House. 
MISS MABEL REBEjLLO: Sir, in the reply, it has been stated that some 
of the Passport Officers have been authorized to issue passports on 'police 
report overdue' basis if the police repo rt is not received within 4 weeks. Why 
only some of the Passport Officers ha ve been authorized? What is the 
criterion? In this way, the people who have known criminal records or who 
are undertrials, have obtained passports without police verification. 
Therefore, police verification should be made mandatory so tha' such people 
are not able to get passports without police verification. What is the policy of 
the Government in this regard? Regular known criminals go abroad, despite 
their passports being impounded. What is the modus operandi that they adopt 
to hoodwink the system? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: The requirement before the. Government is to 
balance between urgent and timely delivery of passports to applicants, 
combined with appropriate an4 proper scrutiny. We have to balance these two 
requirements. We have found that in some States police verification is the 
principal cause of delay. Quite often, it takes 15—20 weeks for the police 
verification to be received by the Passpor t Officer in those States. That is 
why, earlier, a scheme was devised whereby on 'police verification overdue' 
basis, this facility was provided in certain States. This facility was provided, 
combined with a verification that can be  given by a civil servant of a certain 
rank and above. Wc have found that this system has, by and large worked 
satisfactorily. If any adverse report is received from the police after the 
passport is issued on 'police verification due' basis, the passport-holder is 
immediately contacted, he is asked to explain, and wherever necessary, the 
passport is also impounded. The hon. Me mber also wanted to know if there 
are any cases where the passport-holder is able to leave  the country after the 
passport is 
4 

[19 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
impounded. It seems to be very stra nge because after the passport is 
impounded a citizen or whoever it is, is no longer the holder of a valid travel 
document. 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: What will happen if they manage to get a fake 
passport? Many known criminals have gone out, despite the fact that their 
passports had been impounded. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: After the pa ssport is impounded, the necessary 
travel document is not available. No su ch case has come to the notice of the 
Government where even after impounding of the passport, a person is able to 
leave the country. 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: Sir, there is a report in the Hindustan Times, 
dated 6th September, 2000, pointing out how some people had gone to 
Germany from India on fake passports. Here, they could not detect their fake 
passports. Two pages were fake. As soon as they landed in Germany, The 
fake passports were detected and they were sent back. Sir, my second 
supplementary is, a large number of criminals and anti-social elements obtain 
forged passports with the help of the people within the passport office and 
sometimes, with the help of the outside people, that is, agents, travel agents, 
touts etc. If it is so, how many passports have been detected by the 
Government this year? How do you strengthen the investigating and the 
reporting machinery of the Government? How are you making sure that 
innocent people are not harassed by the extra precocious attitude that the 
Government takes? Even if the Government is very cautious, innocent people 
are harassed. But these smart people, anti-social elements, manage to get 
things done. How do you protect the innocent people? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: In two, th ree aspects sought by the hon. 
Member, certain allegations contained in newspapers are quoted by her. I am 
unable to comment on that, Sir, becau se I do not know which particular 
report the hon. Member is referring to. 
On the question of obtaining passports through fraudulent information or 
obtaining fake passports, the hon. Member has made an allegation here that 
passport offices themselves are a party to the issuance of fake passports. Sir, 
no such case has come to the notice of 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2001] 
the Government that the passport office itself is issuing fake passports. But, 
that fake passports are made; yes, we ar e aware of that, Sir, and to safeguard 
against that, a number of additional and special steps have been taken. I will 
not list them here because they are part of the security set-up of the passports 
themselves. So, a number of steps have been taken so as to ensure that the 
whole question of fake passports is controlled. That passports are obtained by 
false information or fraudulent information; yes. That is why police 
verification becomes necessary, and where a passport is urgently needed, etc., 
there, of course, Civil servants of cert ain categories can certify. So, all these 
aspects are there and a balance has to be struck. So far as the point of 
harassment of citizens is concerned, the Government has recently initiated a 
number of steps. And I personally wrote to all the Chief Ministers saying that 
it is the intention of the Government to facilitate the issuance of passports to 
the citizens and, to do so, we, the Government, is ready to make this facility 
available in every district  of the country. We also  want that the passport 
application collection centres should not be in the passport offices only. We 
are ready, in fact, to go even further and assign the task of police verification 
to the District Magistrate or to the Di strict Superintendent of Police and then 
ensure that the passport application is  submitted to the passport offices. I 
have received encouraging response fro m all the States. We have held a 
meeting also because we, th e Government, went so far forward as to say that 
the States could assign and officer whom the Government of India will the 
train at its own cost so that this facility is available to the citizens more 
easily. We have also said that the pass port application forms can be received 
in all speed post offices, and, on a trial basis, we have introduced this facility 
in about 57 metropolitan speed post offices. Now, can I say that it is working 
entirely satisfactorily? Not yet, Sir. We held a training programme for the 
officials assigned by the States, but I am sorry to say that only 14 such 
officials attended the last training programme that we had organized. But we 
will persist with it. The Government is committed to early, harassment-free, 
issuance of passport to a valid applicant who is a citizen of the country, 
simultaneously, ensuring that due

SHRI B.P. SINGHAL: Sir,  there are two kinds of verification when they 
go in the district. One is by the Intelligence Wing of the State, and the other 
is by the District police. I wonder if the Government could consider having 
immediate reports on the basis of the records. That would not delay it at all. 
And, then, subsequently, physical verification could be done by the police by 
visiting either the applicant's village or his house and making inquiries there. 
Would the Government consider having these two things done together so 
that, in one way, it can be speeded up and, at the same time, no wrong person 
gets the passport permanently? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, the hon.  Member would appreciate that 
police verification is a State functi on. The issuance of passport is the 
responsibility and function of the Central Government. 
Sir, in any case, we have to depend  on the State Governments concerned. 
Now, what procedure is adopted by  the State Government to get the 
application verified by the Police is very much the responsibility of the State 
Government. However, to facilitate, to speed up, and to make it more 
efficient, the Central Government has appointed and inter-Ministerial 
Committee which is currently functioning  under the Cabinet Secretariat, and 
is examining all those aspects and additional suggestions as well. 
SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I wish to 
bring to the notice of the hon. Minist er that the problem with the police 
verification of passports in villages is essentially a problem of shortage of 
police personnel, because it is ultimately they who have to go from the thana 
of the village to check up whether the person is there or not. So, is it possible 
for the External Affair's Ministry to liaise with the Home Departments of the 
States to increase the number of police personnel? Sir, we had a meeting of 
the Standing Committee of External Affairs in Calcutta on the same issue, 
and the police, at that time, had been given instructions that they were to 
complete the verification within twenty-one days. At 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2001] 
that time, they literally put their hands up. they said, "we cannot do it with 
the number of people at our disposal". Ultimately, they said, "A practicable 
time limit would be around thirty days." Even that is not practicable. So, 
unless the manpower is increased, I think these delays will continue. I would 
like to know whether the Central Government and the State Governments 
could do something about it. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, we are seized of this aspect of the 
matter. After all, our Passport Offices themselves have a limitation on what 
kind of strength they can have. The question of the strength of police 
personnel in the States is, again, as my learned friend would appreciate, entirely 
a State responsibility. To get out of this kind of a circular situation, these two 
major steps have been initiated — an inter-Ministerial Committee under the 
Cabinet Secretariat — to which I have just referred — has been appointed, 
plus the decentralisation of the passport application procedure has been done, 
taking it down via the speed post to each district, and assigning to the District 
Magistrate or the District Superintendent of Police the task of completing the 
police verification in the District itself before submission of the passport 
application to the Passport Office in th e State concerned. Other than that, as 
far as increasing the strength of the personnel is concerned,at the present 
moment, I regret it is not a practical solution.

in the Net State Domestic product over the period 1993-94 to 1998-99 has 
generally been less for the NE States as compared to other States. (See 
below).

constraints, some of them are beyond th eir capacity to rectify, at least in the 
short or medium term, such as 
• Poor connectivity

• Inadequate infrastructure 
• Less developed formal credit

• Industrial backwardness, and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM 
CHAUHAN): (a) The Sugar Development Fund was formed under the 
provisions of the Sugar Development Fund (SDF) Act, 1982 promulgated on 
20.3.1982, by crediting to the Fund an amount equivalent to the pro ceeds of 
the duty of excise levied and collected under the Sugar Cess Act, 1982, 
reduced by the cost of collection as determined by the Central Government 
after due appropriation made by Parliament by law. The duty of excise levied 
under the Sugar Cess Act, 1982 was Rs. 5.00 per quintal w.e.f. 20.3.1982 
which was enhanced to Rs. 14.00 per quital w.e.f. 29.1Q. 1982 on all sugar 
produced by any sugar factory in India. The balance in the Fund as on 
31.12.2000, net of collections of excise levied under the Sugar Cess Act, 
1982 credited to the Fund, disbursals from the Fund and repayment of loans 
is Rs. 1046.66 crores. 
(b) and (c) The Sugar Development Fu nd Act, 1982 provides that the 
Fund shall be applied for by the Central Government for the following 
purposes:— 
(a) Making loans for facilitating the rehabilitation and modernisation of 
any sugar factory; 
(b) Making loans for the undertaking of any scheme for development of 
sugarcane in the area in which any sugar factory is situated.

3691. SHRI  C.   RAMACHANDRAIAH:  Will the  Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

Members of Parliament and others with regard to the destruction of Buddha

(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it has been urged the demanded that Government urgently 
initiate action with regard to convening of the special session of the U.N. Security 
Council to discuss and take measures for preventing the destructive forces

(d) the details of the action taken by Government in this regard and the 
results thereof?

AFFAIRS (SHRI KRISHNAMRAJU): (a) to (d) The decision of the Taliban 
militia to order the destruction of Buddhist statues in Afghanistan evoked concern 
and disgust and led to the unanimous adoption of a Resolution by both Houses on 
2.3.2001 condemning the Taliban edict. An appeal was made to the World 
community especially the UN to prevail upon the Taliban so that they desist from 
this senseless act of vandalism. 
India took an active part in UN foras on this subject. This included the co-
sponsorship of a UNGA Resolution which was adopted on March 9, 2001, 
calling upon the Taliban to abide by their previous commitments to protect 
Afghanistan's cultural heritage from all acts of vandalism, damage and theft. India 
was also active in UNESCO when the forum was seeking to, prevent the Taliban 
from carrying out the edict. 
The Taliban's obscurantist ideology puts them beyond reason and logic.

3727. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the   norms  prescribed  for  opening  of  the  ESI   hospitals 7 
dispensaries in the country; 
(b) the number of ESI hospitals-dispensar ies opened in Orissa during the 
Ninth Five Year Plan period;

136 

[19 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) the details of the steps taken to upgrade the existing ESI 
hospitals/dispensaries in the State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): (a) to (c) As per the prescribed norms, the ESI Corporation 
constructs four hospital beds per one thousand insured persons. For the sake 
of viability the ESIC generally constructs a minimum fifty bedded hospital at 
the centres having 12,500 Insured Persons (IPs). New ESI Dispensaries are set 
up in the areas having approximately 400 to 1000 IP family units. New ESI 
hospitals/dispensaries are opened on the basis of need and, therefore, not linked 
to five year plans. However, during the period of the Ninth Five Year Plan 
one ESI dispensary at Angul and 2 ESI Hospitals i.e. one each at 
Bhubaneswar and Rourkela were commissioned. 
(d) The provisions of medical care under the ESI Scheme in Orissa are being 
administered by the State Government. However, the expenditure on medical 
care is shared between the ESIC and Govt. of Orissa in the ratio of 7:1. In 
order to bring improvement in the working of the ESI hospitalsftispensaries, the 
ESIC had recently formulated an Action Plan and forwarded the same to the 
State Government including the Government of Orissa for implementation in 
consultation with the ESIC. The Action Plan includes, inter-alia, provision of 
modern equipments in hospitals, supply of necessary basic equipments in all 
dispensaries, establishment of Regional trauma centres, establishment of 
super-speciality services, blood banks, cancer* prevention centres, development 
of indigenous system of medicine etc. An amount of Rs. 245.12 lakh has 
already been sanctioned to the Government of Orissa for procurement of medical 
equipments and other facilities in ESI hospitals'dispensaries. For improving 
the resource position of the State Governments in administration of ESI 
medical care, the ceiling on expenditure on medical care has been enhanced 
from Rs.50(K to Rs.600-'- per Insured Person per annum with effect from

(b) and (c) Under the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972, a

years of qualifying service by giving notice of not less than three months in

qualifying service as on the date of intended retirement shall be increased by 
a period not exceeding five years subj ect to the conditi on that the total 
qualifying service rendered by the Government servant does not in any case 
exceed 33 years and it docs not take hi m beyond the date of superannuation. 
These Rules also provide that if a Go vernment servant, on being declared 
surplus to the establishment in which he was serving, opts to retire 
voluntarily, instead of seeking redeployment, he shall be entitled to have five 
years added to the qualifying service rendered by him subject the condition 
that the qualifying service rendered by such Government servant is not less 
than 15 years on the date on which he

account the said addition is not more  than the service he would have 
rendered had he retired on the date of his superannuation.

existing Voluntary Retirement Scheme, as referred to above, in respect of 
Central Government employees in general. However, the Finance Minister in 
his Budget Speech on 28 February,

(c) if so, the details thereof; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL    
AND    TRAINING    AND    DEPARTMENT    OF 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2001] 
PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS WELFARE OF THE MINISTRY OF 
PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRIMATI 
VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) to (c) The Central Vigilance Commissioner has 
not expressed the view that the existing provisions in the Prevention of 
Corruption Act are too weak to contain corruption though the need for 
enacting a separate legislation for forfeiture of property of corrupt public 
servants has been emphsised by him. 
(d) The Government is fully alive to the need to eradicate corruption at all 
levels of public services. A three pronged strategy of Surveillance, Prevention 
and Punitive/Deterrent action is followed by the Government. Various 
Ministries/Departments/Public Sector Undertakings are responsible to ensure 
probity and integrity in their respective organisations. Recognising that an 
important aspect of this strategy is Preventive Vigilance, steps have been 
taken to ensure transparency in public administration and initiate measures of 
administrative reforms such as introduction of Citizens' Charters, setting up 
of Facilitation Centres etc. The review and simplification of laws, rules and 
procedures has also been taken up. The punitive actions being taken under 
the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 duly supported by various rules 
governing the service conditions of pub lic servants, also acts as a deterrent 
against corruption. However, the drive against corruption in public services to 
check malpractices in administration is  a continumig process. The policies 
formulated in this regard are modified from time to time in order to make 
them more effective and responsive to  the changing environment. Besides, 
some of the recent major initiatives taken by the Government include 
introduction of Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 1999 in Lok Sabha to 
confer statutory status upon the Commission and Freedom of Information 
Bill, 2000 to bring greater transparency  and accountability in the functioning 
of the Government etc.

Decline in GDP 
3756. SHRI K.M. KHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the country is passing through the industrial 
recession; 
(b) if so, the percentage of decline noticed in the target of industrial 
production in the country; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the rate of GDP has also gone down and 
showing negative growth due to slow pace of agricultural production, non-
availability of power and transportation; and 
(d) if so, the steps being taken/proposed to be taken by Government in 
this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) No, Sir. Industrial recession is said to 
occur when there is decline in industrial production in two consecutive 
quarters. This has not happened. However, there has been a slow-down in the 
industrial growth. The increase in the index of Industrial Production during 
April, 2000-February, 2001—the latest period for which data is available—
was 5.1 
175 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2001] 
per cent as compared to 6.5 per cent during the corresponding period of the 
previous year. 
(c) The GDP is not showing negative growth. However, there has been a 
decrease in the rate of growth of GDP. The rate of growth of GDP during the 
financial year 2000-2001 is 6.0 per cent (Advanced Estimates) as compared to 
6.4 per cent (Quick Estimates) during the previous year. 
(d) The performance of the economy is closely monitored and appropriate 
measures taken in the light of the em erging trends as and when necessary. 
Measures being taken are: acceleration of the reforms process in the power 
sector for enhancing private sector investment flow, implementation of the 
National Highway Development Prog ramme (NHDP) thereby accelerating 
the road development programme in the country; reforms in financial sector 
and capital market; reduction in the lending rate of banks and financial 
institutions; further liberalisation in the provisions relating to foreign 
investment to attract FDI, etc.

Failure of Test Flight of GSLV 
3783.  SHRI SURESH PACHOURI:  
SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: 
SHRI ABANI ROY: 
              SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
              SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the first test flight of India's Geosynchronous Satellite 
Launch Vehicle (GSLV) failed to ferry an experimental Satellite in 
the orbit on 28th March, 2001; 
(b) if so, whether the Indian Space Res earch Organisation scientists have 
conducted any preliminary enquiry into this failure, if so, with what results; 
(c) the time ISRO scientists took in developing GSLV and by when the 
same would be ready for launching again in the orbit; and 
(d) to what extent space research prog ramme has been affected and the 
losses suffered on this count and the step s taken to check recurrence of such 
incidents in future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) The first Geosynchronous Satellite 
Launch Vehicle (GSLV-D1) launch attempt was aborted one second before 
the lift-off on 28th March, 2001 by the Automatic Launch Processing System 
after detecting that one of the strap-on boosters did not develop the required 
thrust. 
(b) A 'detailed analysis has been carri ed out about reasons for the strap-on 
motor developing insufficient thrust. The reason for one of the strap-on 
boosters not developing the required thrust is due to a 
204 

[19 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
defective plumbing in the oxidiser flow line of the engine, which had escaped 
detection during testing. This resulted in reduced flow of oxidiser to the 
engine. The anomalous engine has been replaced with a standby engine. AH 
the other systems of the vehicle are found to be healthy. 
(c) The GSLV Project was approved in November, 1990. The GSLV-D1 
has been successfully re-launched on 18th April, 2001. 
(d) The Space Programme has not been af fected by the launch-hold. On 
the other hand, the experience gained through the safe abort and fast recovery 
is invaluable. Launch aborts are intentionally provided for checking the health 
of the launch vehicle during count down for some inadvertent faults. All the 
vehicle systems are healthy and reusable. The disassembled engine also can 
be reused after refurbishment. Hence, the expenditure involved would not also 
be significant. While the quality procedures had been validated through 
realisation of several engines, it is proposed to further strengthen them based 
on the present experience.

Performance of major projects 
3786.   SHRI   OOPALSINH   G.   SOLANKI:   Will  the  PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have recenlty reviewed the performance of major 
projects in various sectors of the States particularly in core sector; 
(b) if so, the outcome thereof, sector-wise, in terms of targets set; 
(c) whether there is any shortfalls in core sector; and 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor and the remedial steps taken by the 
Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS 
AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) As on 1.3.2001, there are 181 major projects in core sectors 
located in different States. Of these, 113 projects have suffered an overall cost 
overrun of 76 per cent with reference to their original cost and 74 projects have 
suffered time overrun ranging from 3 to 168 months with respect to their 
original approved schedule. Against the total original cost of Rs. 1,01,92.19 
crores, the present estimated cost is Rs. 1,39812 crores, which shows an 
escalation of 38 per cent. Sector-wise, cost escalation and range of time overrun 
in seven core sectors is given in the statement. (See below) 
(d) The reasons for shortfalls in execu tion of the projects vary from sector 
to sector as also with regard to the nature of the projects. In general, the 
reasons include delay in land acquisition, late start of work on projects, delay 
in award of work contracts, delay in supply of equipment, poor project 
management and fund constraints. The remedial steps taken to achieve 
targets include: 
(i)  monthly as well as quarterly monitoring by the Government. This 
enables the monitoring agencies to identify constraints and 
help the management in taking remedial measures; 
(ii) indepth   critical   reviews   of   the   progress  by   the   Project

respective State Governments, equipment suppliers, contractors,

turnkey contractors; 
(iv) inter-ministerial coordination and holding facilitation meetings am ong 
concerned parties; 
(v)  setting up of Empowered Committee for speedy resolution of problems of 
contract packages, solving of land acquisition and other problems; and 
(vi) making funds available to complete the projects on schedule.
